status: Selected source-based interpretations, not representative or independently validated ground truth.

cases.name: District of Columbia v. Heller

components.decision: The Court invalidated D.C.’s handgun ban and recognized an individual right to keep a firearm for self-defense at home.
components.scope: The right is not unlimited. This did not invalidate all firearm regulation.
components.survey_fit: Gallup asks about possession generally; Pew asks about sales. Neither isolates D.C.’s home-possession rule or asks whether the Constitution protects it.

components.issue: Keeping a firearm usable for self-defense
components.decision: The Court also invalidated the requirement that lawful firearms at home remain inoperable when needed for self-defense.
components.scope: This is not a ruling against every safe-storage requirement.
components.survey_fit: Neither selected question addresses storage or immediate usability for self-defense.

cases.interpretation_limit: The judgment was 5–4. The two components concern different rules; broad handgun preferences cannot answer both.

cases.name: McDonald v. City of Chicago

components.issue: Applying the right to state and local governments
components.decision: The Court held that the right recognized in Heller applies against state and local governments, reversing and remanding.
components.scope: The case extended the constitutional protection; it did not resolve every local firearm rule.
components.locator: Alito opinion, Parts III–IV; Thomas concurrence.
components.survey_fit: Earlier opposition to handgun bans provides policy context, not an answer to the constitutional incorporation question. Pew’s 2008 observation is reused background, not a new 2010 measurement.

cases.interpretation_limit: Five justices agreed on the result. Four relied on due process; Thomas used the Privileges or Immunities Clause. General policy preferences do not adjudicate that distinction.
